title: The 10% trick
concept: 10% is the foundation of all tip math. Moving the decimal one place left gives you 10% of any number instantly. From there you can build any tip in seconds.
shortcut: 10% of $65 = $6.50 (just move the decimal). Double it for 20% = $13.00. Add half for 15% = $9.75. Master this one move and every tip becomes a two-second calculation.

title: Tipping shortcuts — 15%, 18%, 20%
concept: Every tip percentage builds on 10%. Once you can find 10% instantly (move the decimal left), 20% is double, 15% is 10% plus half, and 18% is 10% + 5% + a small 3% bump. The bigger your bill, the better the $X-per-$100 rule works.
shortcut: Per $100 in bill: 20% = $20, 18% = $18, 15% = $15. For $240, multiply by 2.4. For odd amounts, find 10% first, then build from there. 18% = 10% + 5% + 3%. 20% = double 10%. 15% = 10% + half of 10%.

title: Split any check in your head
concept: Bill splitting isn't a math problem — it's a social moment. Be the person at the table who solves the check in five seconds, while everyone else is still squinting at calculators. The trick: tip the full bill first, then divide. Splitting then tipping shortchanges the server and confuses everyone.
shortcut: Always: Total → add tip → divide by people. A $80 bill, 20% tip = $96, split 4 ways = $24 each. For odd numbers (3 or 5 people), round the per-person share up a dollar — covers the math and the awkward.
example:
Bill: $80.00
20% tip = $16.00
Total = $96.00
Per person (÷ 4) = $24.00

Odd split:
$120 bill, 20% tip = $144
÷ 3 = $48 each

title: The real cost of 'free' deals
concept: 'Free' is rarely free. Buy 2 Get 1 Free is 33% off, not 50%. Buy 1 Get 1 Half Off is 25% off, not 50%. 'Buy 3 for $10' is just a unit-price calculation in disguise. The math the store hopes you skip: per-item cost = total paid ÷ items received.
shortcut: Per-item cost = total paid ÷ items received. B2G1 free: pay 2, get 3, per-item = (2 × price) ÷ 3. B1G1 half off: pay 1.5, get 2, per-item = 0.75 × price. Always ask: do I actually need all of them?
example:
Shampoo $9 each, B2G1 free:
Pay $18 for 3
Per bottle = $6
Real discount = 33%

B1G1 50% off $20:
Pay $30 for 2
Per item = $15
Real discount = 25%

title: Stacking discounts
concept: Two discounts stacked don't add up. 20% off plus 10% off isn't 30% off — the second discount applies to the already-reduced price. You always save a little less than the sum suggests. Before you stack, know the singles: 10% = move decimal, 25% = divide by 4, 50% = halve it.
shortcut: Apply discounts one at a time. $100 → 20% off → $80 → 10% off → $72. Saving: $28, not $30. Quick rule: each 10% combo loses about 1% to stacking. Two 50%-off coupons would only be 75% off, not 100%.

title: Coupon vs cashback — which saves more?
concept: A 20% coupon and 5% cashback aren't the same. The coupon applies to the sticker price. The cashback applies to what you actually pay after the coupon. They stack, but the order matters — coupon first, cashback second, on the smaller amount.
shortcut: Coupon saves: price × coupon%. Cashback saves: (price after coupon) × cashback%. Bigger % almost always wins outright. For stacked deals: do coupon first, cashback on the remainder.
example:
Item $100:
20% coupon = $80 paid
5% cashback on $80 = $4 back
Net cost = $76

Vs no coupon:
5% cashback on $100 = $5
Net cost = $95
Coupon wins by $19

title: What you actually pay: discount + tax
concept: You see '30% off' but you still pay sales tax on the sale price. The checkout total isn't the sticker price. Sale price × (1 + tax%) = real total. Most people forget the tax or apply it to the original price.
shortcut: Discount first, tax second. Never the other way. Sale price = original × (1 − discount%). Final = sale × (1 + tax%). Quick: knock off the discount, add ~10% for tax, check your budget.
example:
$80 shirt, 30% off, 9% tax:
Sale price = $80 × 0.70 = $56
With tax = $56 × 1.09 = $61.04

Forgot the tax? You'd budget $56 and be short $5.

title: Is Uber One / Costco / DashPass worth it?
concept: Membership programs charge a fee for per-use savings. Below break-even, the membership loses money. Above break-even, every additional use is pure savings. The math: break-even uses = fee ÷ saving per use.
shortcut: Break-even uses = fee ÷ per-use saving (round up). If you'll use it more than that in the same period, it pays for itself. DashPass $10/mo saving $3/order → 4 orders/mo breaks even. Order 8/mo → save $14/mo.
example:
DashPass: $10/month, save $3/delivery
Break-even = $10 ÷ $3 = 4 deliveries/mo

Costco: $65/year, save $8/visit
Break-even = $65 ÷ $8 = 9 visits/yr

Uber One: $10/mo, save $2/ride
Break-even = 5 rides/mo

title: Your real subscription bill
concept: Most people have no idea what their subscriptions actually cost annually. $15 Netflix + $11 Spotify + $3 iCloud + $50 gym + $10 DashPass = $89/month — but $1,068/year. Doing the multi-subscription audit is the single most actionable budgeting exercise.
shortcut: Add all your monthly subscriptions, then × 12 for the annual shock number. Round each to the nearest $5 for speed. Drop one? Annual saving = monthly × 12.
example:
Netflix $15 + Spotify $11 + iCloud $3 + gym $50 + DashPass $10 = $89/mo
× 12 = $1,068/year

Drop the gym: save $600/year

title: Is it actually worth it?
concept: The real cost of anything isn't the sticker price — it's the cost per use. A $120 yoga unlimited pass used 4 times = $30/class (worse than drop-in). A $200 espresso machine used 300 times = $0.67/cup (way better than café). Cost-per-use turns 'is this a good deal?' into a calculation.
shortcut: Cost per use = total price ÷ estimated uses. Compare to your alternative. Estimate uses HONESTLY — most people overestimate how often they'll use things. Unlimited yoga at $120: need 8+ classes vs $18 drop-ins.
example:
Yoga unlimited: $120/mo
4 classes → $30/class
12 classes → $10/class
Drop-in: $18 each
Worth it above 7 classes

Espresso machine: $200
300 cups → $0.67/cup
Café: $4.50/cup
Saves $1,149/yr

title: Tax, totals, and budget checks
concept: Sales tax in the US is usually 6-10% depending on your state. Two things confuse people: applying the tax to the right base, and the asymmetry that subtracting 10% from a budget doesn't give you the pre-tax max. To go from a post-tax budget to pre-tax: divide by (1 + tax%).
shortcut: Adding tax: price × (1 + tax%). Finding pre-tax max from a budget: budget ÷ (1 + tax%) — NOT budget × (1 − tax%). The asymmetry is small but real: $100 budget at 10% tax → max pre-tax is $90.91, not $90.
example:
$40 item, 8% tax:
10% of $40 = $4
Minus 20% = $0.80 off
Tax ≈ $3.20
Total ≈ $43.20

Budget $100, 10% tax:
Max pre-tax = $100 ÷ 1.10 = $90.91
NOT $90 (which gives $99 total)

title: The 50/30/20 rule
concept: The simplest budgeting framework that actually works: 50% of after-tax income to needs (rent, food, transport, insurance, minimum debt), 30% to wants (dining out, entertainment, subscriptions), 20% to savings and debt payoff. The math is simple — the insight is most people have never calculated their own ratios.
shortcut: Half / a third / a fifth of take-home. Quick check: take-home × 0.5 = your needs ceiling. If rent alone exceeds that, your budget is structurally stressed.
example:
Take-home: $4,200/month
Needs: $2,100 (50%)
Wants: $1,260 (30%)
Savings: $840 (20%)

Rent of $2,400? Already above 50% — wants or savings must shrink.

title: Small daily purchases, big annual cost
concept: The latte factor: small daily expenses compound into shocking annual numbers. A $5.50 daily coffee = $2,008/year. A $12 daily workday lunch = $3,120/year. Knowing the annual number makes the daily decision honest.
shortcut: Daily × 365 for every-day habits. Workday × 260 for workday-only habits. Want weekly? × 7. Round up for budgeting.
example:
Daily coffee $5.50:
× 365 = $2,008/year

Workday lunch $12:
× 260 = $3,120/year

Drop both, brew + pack:
Save $3,000+/year

title: Why your budget is always short
concept: Multiplying weekly cost by 4 gives you a 48-week year — you're missing 4 weeks of expenses annually. A $85/week grocery budget × 4 = $340/month, but the real monthly figure is $85 × 4.33 = $368. Over a year, the wrong multiplier underestimates by ~$336.
shortcut: Weekly × 4.33 (= 52 ÷ 12) for monthly. Biweekly × 2.17 (= 26 ÷ 12). Always round up if budgeting. Monthly → weekly: ÷ 4.33.
example:
Weekly grocery: $85
Wrong (×4): $340/month
Right (×4.33): $368/month

Annual shortfall from ×4: $85 × 52 − ($340 × 12) = $4,420 − $4,080 = $340/year

Biweekly pay $1,800:
Monthly = $1,800 × 2.17 = $3,906

title: Gross vs net — what you actually keep
concept: Your gross pay is what you earn before taxes. Net pay is what arrives in your bank account. Between federal tax, state tax, Social Security, and Medicare, most workers keep 70–75 cents of every dollar earned. Always plan your budget with net, never gross.
shortcut: Quick estimate: take 25–30% off gross to get net. Earning $3,000/month gross? Expect $2,100–$2,250 net. For annual salary: divide by 12 to get monthly gross, then knock off 25–30% for a working budget number.
example:
Gross pay: $3,000/month
−25% deductions = $750
Net pay ≈ $2,250

$60,000 salary
÷ 12 = $5,000/month gross
−25% = $3,750 net

title: What a % raise really adds
concept: A percentage raise sounds exciting, but the real number is what lands in your paycheck. A 5% raise on $60,000 is $3,000 more per year — about $250/month before taxes. Knowing the actual dollar impact helps you negotiate and plan clearly.
shortcut: Annual raise = current salary × raise%. Monthly bump = ÷ 12. After-tax: × 0.72 (assumes ~28% total deductions). 5% on $65k = $3,250/yr → $271/mo gross → ~$195/mo in your pocket.
example:
Salary: $60,000
5% raise = $3,000/year
Per month = $250
After tax ≈ $175/month

title: Overtime pay — time and a half
concept: Overtime in the US is 1.5× your regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 per week. Those extra hours pay significantly more — 8 hours of overtime at $20/hr earns you $240, not $160.
shortcut: Overtime rate = regular × 1.5. Overtime pay = OT hours × OT rate. Total week: (40 × regular) + (OT hours × regular × 1.5). At $20/hr working 47 hours: $800 + (7 × $30) = $1,011 gross.
example:
Regular rate: $20/hr
Overtime rate: $20 × 1.5 = $30/hr
8 OT hours × $30 = $240
Vs. 8 regular hours = $160

title: Compare any two paychecks
concept: Job offers come in different pay periods — weekly, bi-weekly, monthly, annual. Bi-weekly is 26 paychecks/year (not 24). To compare any two offers fairly, convert both to annual first. The most expensive mistake: treating bi-weekly as semi-monthly (24 vs 26) — you under-count two paychecks.
shortcut: Annual ÷ 52 = weekly. Annual ÷ 26 = bi-weekly. Annual ÷ 12 = monthly. To compare offers: annualize each, then subtract. $1,150/week vs $4,800/month? $59,800 vs $57,600 — weekly wins by $2,200.

title: Is your raise actually a raise?
concept: A 3% raise sounds great until inflation is 4%. Your purchasing power actually decreased. Real raise = nominal raise − inflation rate. If inflation outpaces your raise, you're effectively taking a pay cut — you can buy less with your new salary than you could before.
shortcut: Real raise % = raise % − inflation %. Real dollar change = salary × real raise %. A 3% raise with 4% inflation: real change = −1%, meaning you lost purchasing power. Always compare your raise to the current inflation rate.
example:
Salary: $65,000
Raise: 3% = $1,950
Inflation: 4% = $2,600
Real change: −$650/year
You're actually losing money

title: Hourly to salary in 2 seconds
concept: Full-time work is roughly 2,000 hours per year (40 hrs × 50 weeks). The mental math: double your hourly rate, add three zeros. $25/hr → double → $50 → add three zeros → $50,000/year. To reverse: drop three zeros, halve. $70,000 → $70 → halve → $35/hr.
shortcut: Hourly to annual: double + three zeros. Annual to hourly: drop three zeros, halve. Works because 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 hours. For part-time, scale: 1,500 hrs = double + 1,500.
example:
Hourly to annual:
$18/hr → $36,000
$32/hr → $64,000

Annual to hourly:
$50,000 → $25/hr
$80,000 → $40/hr

Compare offer:
$28/hr ≈ $56k vs $52k salaried
Hourly wins by $4k

title: Your salary isn't your compensation
concept: Total compensation = base salary + employer-paid health insurance + 401k match + bonus + stock. For most jobs, total comp is 15-25% higher than base. A $70k base with $8k insurance + $3k match + $5k bonus = $86k total comp. When comparing offers, compare total comp.
shortcut: Add 15-25% to base for a rough total comp estimate. Employer pays $500/mo for your insurance? That's $6k/yr of compensation you never see in your paycheck.
example:
Offer A: $75k base + $6k insurance + $2k match = $83k total
Offer B: $80k base + $3k insurance + $1k match = $84k total

B wins by $1k — barely. A might have better benefits in practice.

title: Is your side hustle actually worth it?
concept: Effective hourly rate = (earnings − expenses) ÷ total hours including prep, travel, admin. A $200 weekend gig that takes 12 hours and costs $30 in gas is really $14.17/hr — half of what a $28/hr day job pays. Side hustles often look better than they pay.
shortcut: Net earnings ÷ total hours including everything. Compare to your day job hourly equivalent (annual ÷ 2,000). If side hustle pays < 70% of day rate, the time is better spent on rest, a promotion, or a second skill.
example:
Side hustle:
$200 gig
12 hours total
$30 gas
Effective: $14.17/hr

Day job:
$55,000 ÷ 2,000 = $27.50/hr

Gap: $13.33/hr
Side hustle pays 51% of day job — worth it?

title: The Rule of 72 — when does it double?
concept: The Rule of 72 is a mental math shortcut: divide 72 by the annual interest rate to estimate how many years it takes for money to double. It works for any growth rate — investment returns, debt interest, even inflation.
shortcut: Years to double = 72 ÷ annual rate. At 8%: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. At 6%: 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. At 12%: 72 ÷ 12 = 6 years. Works equally well in reverse: if something doubles in 10 years, the implied rate is ~7.2%.
example:
Savings at 4%/year:
72 ÷ 4 = 18 years to double

Debt at 12%/year:
72 ÷ 12 = 6 years to double
(if you only pay minimums)

title: ROI — the one number that compares anything
concept: Return on investment is the universal scale: what % did you gain relative to what you put in? A kitchen renovation ($15k → $20k home value) is 33% ROI. An index fund averages 10%/year. A $200 course leading to a $5k raise is 2,400% ROI. ROI lets you compare wildly different decisions on the same axis.
shortcut: ROI% = (gain ÷ cost) × 100. Universal comparison: kitchen reno 33%, course 2,400%, index fund 10%/yr. But ROI isn't always the answer — a $3k vacation has 0% financial ROI but priceless life ROI.

title: 401(k) match — free money math
concept: Many employers match your 401(k) contributions up to a percentage of your salary. If your employer matches 50% up to 6% of your salary, and you contribute 6%, they add an extra 3%. Not contributing enough to get the full match is literally leaving free money on the table.
shortcut: Match amount = your contribution × match rate. If you earn $60,000 and contribute 6% ($3,600), a 50% match gives you $1,800 free. Total going into your 401(k): $5,400. Always contribute at least enough to max the match.
example:
Salary: $60,000
You contribute 6% = $3,600
Employer matches 50% = $1,800
Total: $5,400/year

title: Roth vs Traditional IRA
concept: Both IRAs cap at $7,000/year (2025) or $8,000 if you're 50+. Roth uses after-tax dollars; Traditional uses pre-tax. The Roth's killer feature: tax-free growth AND tax-free withdrawals. Income above $150k single / $236k married phases out direct Roth contributions. Under 35 in a lower bracket? Roth usually wins — decades of tax-free growth on top of tax-free withdrawals is enormous.
shortcut: Roth contribution = your cash. Tax saving (Traditional) = contribution × tax rate. Roth's hidden win: $7k/yr at 22% bracket growing to $475k over 25 years = $0 tax on withdrawal vs $114k tax in a Traditional. Under 35 + lower bracket = Roth. Peak earning years = Traditional.
example:
$5,000 contribution at 22% tax rate:
Roth: pay $1,100 tax now
Traditional: save $1,100 now, owe tax later

Growth advantage:
$7k/yr × 25 yrs grows to $475k Roth
→ $0 tax on withdrawal
Traditional at 24% = $114k tax bill

title: Compound growth over time
concept: Compound growth is your money earning money on its earnings. $500/month at 8% grows to $91k in 10 years, $296k in 20, $745k in 30. The longer your time horizon, the more of your final balance is interest (not contributions). Time matters more than amount.
shortcut: Total contributed = monthly × 12 × years. At 8% growth, multiplier is ~1.5× in 10 yrs, ~2.5× in 20, ~4.5× in 30. % of balance that's interest: 33% at 10 yrs, 60% at 20 yrs, 78% at 30 yrs. Start early — every decade roughly doubles your money via compounding.
example:
$500/month × 20 years:
Contributed: $120,000
Grew to: $296,000
Interest: $176,000 (60% of balance)

Start at 25 vs 35 (both stop at 65):
25 → $1.3M
35 → $570k
Gap from 10 years: $730k

title: The power of investing every month
concept: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals — buying more shares when prices are low, fewer when high. Over time your average cost per share lands lower than the average market price. The behavior beats the math: people who try to time the market typically lose to people who just keep buying.
shortcut: Total invested = monthly amount × months. Shares per month = amount ÷ price that month. Average cost = total invested ÷ total shares. DCA wins on volatility — when prices dip, your fixed dollars buy more shares.
example:
Invest $500/month × 12 = $6,000
Prices vary $40-60/share
Total shares: ~125
Avg cost: $48/share
Market avg: $50/share
You paid less because you bought more when cheap.

title: The fee that eats your retirement
concept: A 1% expense ratio sounds small. On $100k it's $1,000/year — but the real cost is the compounding you lose. Over 30 years at 8% growth, that 1% fee costs you roughly $200,000 in lost final balance. The gap between a 0.03% index fund and a 1% managed fund is staggering.
shortcut: Annual fee = portfolio × expense ratio. Quick rule: every 0.5% in fees costs about 10% of your final balance over 30 years. Choose funds with expense ratios under 0.2% wherever possible.
example:
$100k portfolio, 1% expense ratio:
Annual fee: $1,000

$200k portfolio, 0.5% vs 0.05%:
Diff: 0.45% × $200k = $900/yr
Over 30 yrs ≈ $50k+ lost

Always check expense ratios.

title: How much emergency fund do you actually need?
concept: 3-6 months of ESSENTIAL expenses — not income. Essential means rent, food, insurance, transport, debt minimums. Not subscriptions, dining out, entertainment. Most people calculate against income and get an overwhelming number; calculating against essentials makes the goal achievable.
shortcut: Sum your 4-5 non-negotiable monthly bills. That's your essential number. × 3 = minimum target, × 6 = solid. Months of runway = current savings ÷ essentials. Cut $X from non-essentials = (savings ÷ (essentials − cut)) months of runway.
example:
Essentials:
Rent $1,500 + food $400 + insurance $200 + transport $200 + debt min $300 = $2,600/month

Target (6 months): $15,600
You have $9,800 saved.
Runway: $9,800 ÷ $2,600 = 3.8 months

title: Rental yield — is the property worth it?
concept: Gross rental yield = (annual rent ÷ purchase price) × 100. Below 5% is weak (you're banking on appreciation), 6-8% is solid, 8%+ is strong. Net yield deducts management (typically 10%) and vacancy (typically 8%). A property with great location but low yield is a speculation, not an investment.
shortcut: Quick check: monthly rent × 12 ≥ 5% of price? If not, skip. Net yield = gross × (1 − mgmt% − vacancy%). At 10% mgmt + 8% vacancy, you keep 82% of gross.
example:
$300k property, $2,000/month rent:
Annual rent: $24,000
Gross yield: 8%
Net (after 10% mgmt + 8% vacancy):
8% × 0.82 = 6.6% net

Solid investment — gross above 5%, net above 6%.

title: Am I on track? The retirement savings check
concept: Fidelity's age-based rule: 1× salary saved by 30, 3× by 40, 6× by 50, 10× by 67. Calculate your 'savings multiple' (current savings ÷ current salary) and compare to your age target. If behind, increase your contribution by 1% of salary each year until you catch up.
shortcut: Multiple = savings ÷ salary. Age 30 target = 1×. Age 35 = 2×. Age 40 = 3×. Gap (in dollars) = (target multiple × salary) − current savings. Monthly to close in N years = gap ÷ (N × 12).
example:
Age 35, salary $65k, saved $80k:
Multiple = $80k ÷ $65k = 1.23×
Target at 35: ~2×
Gap: (2 × $65k) − $80k = $50k

Close in 5 years: $50k ÷ 60 months = $833/mo extra savings

title: How credit card interest works
concept: Credit card APR sounds small — 20% — but it compounds monthly. The interest charge each month is APR ÷ 12 × balance. On a $2,000 balance at 20% APR you're paying ~$33 every single month just in interest.
shortcut: Monthly interest = balance × APR% ÷ 12. To estimate: move the decimal left two places (gives 1%), multiply by your APR, divide by 12. $2,000 × 20% ÷ 12 = $33.33/month.

title: The minimum payment trap
concept: Credit card minimum payments are usually 2% of your balance. They feel manageable — but they're designed to keep you in debt longer. A $3,000 balance at 2% minimum means paying only $60/month while interest charges eat most of it.
shortcut: Minimum payment ≈ balance × 2%. Always pay more than the minimum. Even an extra $50/month can cut years off your payoff timeline.
example:
Balance: $3,000
Minimum = $3,000 × 2% = $60
At 20% APR, interest alone = $50/month
Only $10 goes to principal!

title: The true cost of a loan
concept: The sticker price of a loan is not what you pay. Total = monthly payment × number of months. The difference between that and your original loan is the lender's profit — pure interest. The 'interest tax' = total interest ÷ loan amount. Above 15%? Question whether you really need to borrow.
shortcut: Total cost = payment × months. Interest = total − loan. Interest tax % = interest ÷ loan × 100. A $6k loan costing $1,200 interest = 20% interest tax. Save and pay cash if you can spread the wait over 12 months.
example:
Loan: $6,000
Payment: $200/month × 36 months
Total: $7,200
Interest: $1,200
Interest tax: 20%

Save $250/month for 24 months:
You'd have $6,000 cash, save $1,200

title: Debt-to-income ratio
concept: DTI ratio = total monthly debt payments ÷ monthly income × 100. Lenders use this to assess risk. Under 36% is healthy; over 43% is a red flag for mortgage approval. It tells you how much of your income is already spoken for.
shortcut: DTI% = monthly debt ÷ monthly income × 100. If you earn $5,000/month and pay $1,500 in debt: $1,500 ÷ $5,000 × 100 = 30% DTI. Keep it under 36%.
example:
Monthly income: $5,000
Debt payments: $1,500
DTI = $1,500 ÷ $5,000 × 100 = 30%

title: The power of extra payments
concept: Every extra dollar you pay toward debt saves you that dollar's worth of future interest. The annual interest saving from an extra monthly payment equals extra payment × APR%. Small extra payments compound over time into big savings.
shortcut: Annual interest saved ≈ extra payment × APR%. Paying an extra $100/month on a 20% APR card saves $20/year per $100 — plus you reduce the principal faster, which shrinks future interest too.
example:
Extra payment: $100 · APR: 20%
Annual saving ≈ $100 × 20% = $20
Plus reduced principal each month

title: Pay off debt faster: avalanche vs snowball
concept: Avalanche: pay minimums on all debts, throw extra money at the highest-interest one first. Saves the most money mathematically. Snowball: pay minimums on all, throw extra at the smallest balance first. Gives quicker psychological wins. Avalanche always wins on math; snowball often wins on behavior.
shortcut: Avalanche: target the highest APR first. Snowball: target the smallest balance first. Interest saved by putting $X extra against the higher rate vs lower rate: $X × (highRate − lowRate) ÷ 12 per month. The difference between avalanche and snowball over time = your 'psychology premium.'
example:
Debt A: $5k at 24% APR
Debt B: $2k at 18% APR

Avalanche: pay extra on A → saves more interest
$200 extra: $200 × (24% − 18%) ÷ 12 = $1/month saved
× 24 months = $24 psychology premium

Snowball pays off B first (motivating!), then A.

title: APR vs APY — the number banks hide
concept: APR is the simple annual rate. APY includes the effect of compounding. A 20% APR card compounded monthly = ~21.9% APY. Banks always show whichever number looks better for them: APY on savings (higher), APR on loans (lower). The compounding gap is real money.
shortcut: APY ≈ APR + (APR² ÷ 200) for monthly compounding. 20% APR → 20 + (400 ÷ 200) = 22% APY. Monthly rate on a loan = APR ÷ 12. Annual interest cost = balance × APY ÷ 100 (not APR).
example:
Card with 24% APR:
Monthly rate: 24% ÷ 12 = 2%
APY: 24 + (576 ÷ 200) = 26.88%

On $5,000 balance held a year:
Using APR: $1,200 interest
Using APY: $1,344 interest (real)
Difference: $144 hidden

title: Buy Now, Pay Later — the math they don't show
concept: BNPL splits a purchase into 4 'easy payments.' Sounds free. Miss one payment = up to $35 late fee (sometimes 25% of the missed payment). On a $300 purchase that's an 11.7% surcharge. The real danger: stacking 3-4 BNPL plans creates invisible debt — none of it on your credit card statement. Research: 49% of BNPL users report financial problems, 24% have missed at least one payment.
shortcut: Total BNPL = number of payments × payment amount. Surcharge from one late fee = lateFee ÷ originalPrice × 100. Stacked monthly burden = sum of all your BNPL payments. If you can't pay cash today, you can't afford it.
example:
$300 item, 4 × $75 BNPL:
Miss one: $35 late fee
Total paid: $335
Surcharge: 11.7%

Stacked plans:
$75 (item A) + $50 (item B) + $40 (item C) = $165/mo invisible debt

title: Rent affordability (28% rule)
concept: The 28% rule says your rent shouldn't exceed 28% of your gross monthly income. It's a quick gut check when apartment shopping — if a place costs more than 28% of what you earn before taxes, it's going to squeeze your budget.
shortcut: Max rent = monthly gross × 0.28. Reverse: min income for a given rent = rent ÷ 0.28. For $5,000/month: max rent = $1,400. For $2,000 rent: need $7,143/month gross = $85,714/year.
example:
Monthly salary: $5,000
Max rent: $5,000 × 28% = $1,400

title: Rent increase math
concept: When your landlord raises rent by a percentage, the dollar impact depends on your current rent. National average increase is 3-5% — anything above 5% is aggressive. The renewal-vs-move decision often comes down to: how many months of higher rent equals the cost of moving?
shortcut: Increase $ = rent × increase%. Compare to 4% average to spot aggressive hikes. Renewal-vs-move: moving cost ÷ monthly increase = months until staying costs more.
example:
$1,500 rent, 7% increase:
$105 more/mo, $1,260/yr
7% vs avg 4% = aggressive

Move costs $4,200, increase $120/mo:
Break-even: $4,200 ÷ $120 = 35 months
If lease is 12 months, staying is cheaper.

title: Move-in cost calculator
concept: Moving into a new place often requires first month's rent, last month's rent, and a security deposit upfront. Some cities add broker fees. The total can be 3–4× your monthly rent, which catches people off guard.
shortcut: Move-in = first + last + deposit (+ broker fee). For $1,800/month with a broker fee equal to one month's rent: $1,800 × 4 = $7,200 due before you get the keys.
example:
Rent: $1,800/month
First + last + deposit + broker
$1,800 × 4 = $7,200 move-in

title: The roommate math — $6,500/year
concept: A roommate is the single biggest housing decision for renters. A 2025 study across 100 US cities found splitting a 2BR vs renting a 1BR solo saves an average of $541/month — $6,500/year — and that's before utilities, internet, and household supplies (which also split). In some cities you save 48%.
shortcut: Annual saving = (1BR + 1BR utilities) − (shared 2BR + 2BR utilities) / 2. Unequal split? Bigger bedroom = 55%, smaller = 45%. Most apartment splits should be slightly uneven based on room size.
example:
1BR alone: $1,800 rent + $200 util = $2,000/mo
2BR shared: $2,400 rent + $250 util
Your half: $1,325/mo
Savings: $675/mo, $8,100/yr

Unequal split (bigger room):
2BR $2,400 × 55% = $1,320 for you

title: What renting actually costs you each month
concept: Rent is the headline number, not the actual cost. The true monthly housing cost = rent + renter's insurance + utilities + parking + laundry + commute. Typically 15-25% more than rent alone. The 28% rule should be applied to TOTAL housing cost, not just rent.
shortcut: Add all housing-adjacent monthly bills. That's your real monthly housing cost. Quick add-on rule: rent × 1.20 ≈ true cost for most renters. Apply 28% rule to THAT, not the rent alone.
example:
Rent: $1,500
Insurance: $15
Utilities: $150
Parking: $100
Laundry: $40
True cost: $1,805/mo (+20%)

Income $5,500: 28% cap = $1,540
Apartment 'fits' at rent — fails on true cost.

title: Mortgage payment, the right way
concept: Mental-math mortgage estimates: at 5% over 30 years, payment ≈ loan × 0.00537. At 6%, × 0.006. At 7%, × 0.00665. These factors come from actual amortization — they're accurate within $5 on typical loans. Old shortcut (interest + principal portions) overestimates by ~30%.
shortcut: At 6% over 30 yrs: monthly ≈ loan × 0.006. At 5%: × 0.0054. At 7%: × 0.0067. Per $100k borrowed at 6%: $600/mo. $300k loan? $1,800/mo. Add ~$300 for property tax + insurance.
example:
$300,000 mortgage at 6%, 30 years:
$300k × 0.006 = $1,800/mo
Actual amortized: $1,799 ✓

Vs renting $1,900?
P&I cheaper by $100
+ tax/insurance ~$300 = $2,100
Rent slightly cheaper

title: Should I break my lease? The math
concept: Early termination fees average 2-4 months' rent. Add moving costs ($1,200-$2,500). Compare to: how much you'd save monthly at the new place × remaining months on lease. If break cost > near-term savings, stay.
shortcut: Total break cost = months penalty × rent + moving cost. Break-even = break cost ÷ monthly saving. If lease has fewer months left than break-even, staying is cheaper.
example:
Lease: 8 months left at $1,800
Break fee: 2 months = $3,600
Moving: $1,200
Total break cost: $4,800

New apartment: $1,500/mo ($300 saving)
Break-even: $4,800 ÷ $300 = 16 months
Only 8 left → STAY, save $2,400

title: Marginal tax brackets
concept: Tax brackets are marginal — you don't pay your top rate on all your income. Only the income above each bracket's threshold gets taxed at the higher rate. Being 'in the 22% bracket' means only your dollars above that threshold are taxed at 22%.
shortcut: Tax = (income up to bracket 1) × rate 1 + (remaining income) × rate 2. On $60,000 with a 10% bracket up to $40,000 and 22% above: ($40,000 × 10%) + ($20,000 × 22%) = $4,000 + $4,400 = $8,400.

title: Paycheck deductions
concept: Your gross pay gets reduced by FICA (Social Security + Medicare = 7.65%), federal income tax, and state income tax before you see a dime. Understanding these deductions helps you predict your actual take-home pay from any job offer.
shortcut: Net pay = gross × (1 − total deduction rate). If FICA is 7.65%, federal is 12%, and state is 5%, total rate = 24.65%. From $4,000 gross: $4,000 × 0.7535 = $3,014 net.

title: Your tax refund is not a bonus
concept: A $3,000 refund means you gave the government a $250/month interest-free loan all year. That's not a windfall — it's your own money returned without interest. If you'd adjusted your W-4 and invested $250/month at 6% instead, you'd have ~$3,100 by year-end — more than the refund.
shortcut: Refund ÷ pay periods = how much extra you should have kept per paycheck. Refund × ~3% = roughly what you forfeited in lost growth over the year. Big refund = poorly-set W-4, not a bonus.
example:
Refund: $3,000
Monthly over-withholding: $250

If invested at 6%/yr:
~$3,100 at year-end
Extra ~$100 vs lump refund

Over 10 years of same pattern:
Forfeited >$1,000 in compounding

title: Self-employment tax
concept: Freelancers and gig workers pay both halves of FICA (15.3% total) plus regular income tax. Worse: there's no employer withholding, so the IRS requires quarterly estimated payments (April, June, Sept, Jan). Skip them and pay a penalty.
shortcut: Set aside 30-35% of every freelance check (covers SE 15.3% + income tax ~15-20%). Quarterly estimated payment = quarterly income × combined rate. $8k earned in a quarter at 30% combined = $2,400 to the IRS.
example:
$5,000 freelance income:
SE tax: 15.3% = $765
+ income tax ~15-20%
Set aside: $1,500-$1,750

Quarterly:
$8,000/quarter at 30% combined
= $2,400 estimated payment due

title: Standard vs itemized — which saves you more?
concept: The standard deduction is $15,200 single / $30,400 married (2025). Itemize if mortgage interest + state/local taxes + charity exceeds that. After the 2017 tax law, ~90% of filers take the standard. Homeowners with mortgages and high-tax-state residents (NY, CA, NJ) often benefit from itemizing.
shortcut: Add mortgage interest + state taxes + charity. If > $15,200 single (or $30,400 married), itemize. Tax saving vs standard = (itemized − standard) × your tax rate.
example:
Single, 22% tax bracket:
Mortgage interest: $9,400
State taxes: $5,100
Charity: $1,800
Itemized: $16,300
Standard: $15,200
Extra saving: $1,100 × 22% = $242

title: Sell too soon, pay double the tax
concept: Short-term capital gains (held < 1 year) are taxed at your ordinary income rate (22-24% for most). Long-term gains (held > 1 year) are taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20%. For most of the target audience, the gap is ~7 percentage points. Waiting a few weeks past the 1-year mark can save thousands.
shortcut: On a $10k gain at 22% ordinary rate: short-term = $2,200 tax. Long-term at 15% = $1,500. Wait one extra month = save $700. Per $10k of gain, waiting saves ~$700.
example:
Held stock 11 months, $15k gain:
Sell now (short-term, 24%):
$15k × 24% = $3,600 tax

Wait 1 more month (long-term, 15%):
$15k × 15% = $2,250 tax
Save: $1,350

title: Stop lending the government your money
concept: Your W-4 determines how much tax is withheld per paycheck. If you consistently get a refund over $500, you're over-withholding — handing the government an interest-free loan. Reducing withholding by refund ÷ pay periods means more cash each paycheck that you can invest or save.
shortcut: Last year's refund ÷ pay periods = bump per paycheck. $3,000 refund ÷ 26 biweekly = $115/check extra. Invested at 6%/year, that compounds to slightly MORE than the refund within a year.
example:
Refund: $3,000
Biweekly paychecks: 26
Per-paycheck bump: $115

Invest $115/check at 6%:
Year-end value: ~$3,100
Vs lump refund $3,000
Gain: ~$100 + control of cash

title: Deductible vs premium tradeoff
concept: Your premium is the floor — what you pay every month no matter what. Your deductible adds to your ceiling — the worst-case annual exposure if something major happens. Higher deductible = lower floor but higher ceiling. This is the simplified model; lessons 2-3 add coinsurance and the OOP cap.
shortcut: Floor (best-case annual) = premium × 12. Ceiling (simplified worst-case) = floor + deductible. Range = deductible. That range is your financial exposure if you have a bad year.
example:
Plan A: $350/mo, $1,000 deductible
Floor: $4,200/year (healthy year)
Ceiling: $5,200 (full deductible spent)
Exposure: $1,000

Plan B: $250/mo, $3,000 deductible
Floor: $3,000
Ceiling: $6,000
Exposure: $3,000

title: Copay vs coinsurance
concept: A copay is a flat fee per visit ($30 per doctor visit). Coinsurance is a percentage of the bill you pay after the deductible is met (you pay 20%, insurance pays 80%). On expensive procedures, coinsurance adds up fast — 20% of a $10,000 surgery is $2,000.
shortcut: Your coinsurance cost = total bill × your coinsurance %. On a $5,000 bill with 20% coinsurance: $5,000 × 20% = $1,000 out of your pocket.
example:
Surgery: $8,000
Deductible already met
Coinsurance: 20%
You pay: $8,000 × 20% = $1,600
Insurance pays: $6,400

title: Out-of-pocket maximum
concept: The out-of-pocket max is your safety net — the most you'll pay in a year. Once you hit it, insurance covers 100%. Total out-of-pocket = deductible + coinsurance payments, capped at the OOP max. If your OOP max is $6,000, that's your absolute worst-case annual expense.
shortcut: After deductible, you pay coinsurance until you hit the OOP max. On a $50,000 hospital stay with $2,000 deductible and $6,000 OOP max: you pay at most $6,000, insurance covers the rest.
example:
Hospital bill: $50,000
Deductible: $2,000
Coinsurance: 20%
OOP max: $6,000
You pay: $6,000 (capped)
Insurance: $44,000

title: HDHP vs PPO comparison
concept: A High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) has lower premiums but higher deductibles. A PPO has higher premiums but lower out-of-pocket costs. HDHPs make sense if you're healthy and rarely use healthcare. PPOs win if you have regular medical needs or expect major procedures.
shortcut: HDHP total = lower premium × 12 + higher deductible. PPO total = higher premium × 12 + lower deductible. If HDHP worst-case < PPO worst-case, HDHP saves money. Also: HDHPs qualify for HSAs.
example:
HDHP: $200/mo, $3,000 deductible
Worst case: $5,400

PPO: $400/mo, $500 deductible
Worst case: $5,300

PPO wins by $100 in worst case
but HDHP saves $2,400 if healthy

title: HSA triple tax advantage
concept: HSAs have the triple tax advantage: contributions are pre-tax (reduce taxable income), growth is tax-free, withdrawals for medical are tax-free. The hidden superpower: after age 65, you can withdraw HSA funds for ANY purpose (just pay income tax, like a Traditional IRA). Medical withdrawals stay tax-free at any age. This makes the HSA arguably the best retirement account in the tax code.
shortcut: Annual tax saving = contribution × your tax rate. Long-term: HSA grows like an investment account. $3,500/yr from 30 to 65 at 7% growth = ~$550,000, all tax-free for medical or income-taxed for anything else.
example:
Contribute $3,000 at 22% rate:
Tax saving: $660 immediate

Long-term:
$3,500/yr × 35 yrs at 7%
= ~$550,000
Used for medical: $0 tax
Used for retirement (after 65): income tax

title: FSA: free money or wasted money?
concept: Flexible Spending Accounts are use-it-or-lose-it: any unspent balance at year-end disappears (some plans allow $640 rollover or 2.5-month grace period). The tax savings = election × your tax rate. If you elect $2,850 at a 25% bracket, you save $712 in tax. But if you only spend $1,800, you forfeit $1,050 — for a net loss of $338.
shortcut: Only elect what you'll definitely spend. Tax savings = election × tax rate. Break-even: spend at least (1 − tax rate) of your election. In a 25% bracket, you need to spend at least 75% of what you elect to come out ahead.
example:
Election: $2,850 at 25% bracket
Tax savings: $712

Scenario A: Spend $2,850 → save $712 ✓
Scenario B: Spend $1,800 → save $712 in tax but lose $1,050 unused
Net: −$338

title: How much life insurance do you actually need?
concept: Two methods: (1) The 10-12× rule of thumb — multiply annual income by 10. (2) DIME method: Debt + Income replacement + Mortgage + Education costs. Add mortgage balance, subtract savings/existing coverage. Term life (20-30 years) is what most young families need — way cheaper than whole life.
shortcut: Quick estimate: salary × 10 = baseline coverage. Adjusted: + mortgage − savings. Compare two quotes by the annual cost per $100k of coverage.
example:
Salary: $70,000
10× rule: $700,000 baseline
Mortgage: +$280,000
Savings: −$50,000
Adjusted: $930,000 needed

Term quotes (30yr, healthy 35yo):
$500k @ $35/mo = $420/yr
$1M @ $55/mo = $660/yr

title: Brand name vs generic — the prescription math
concept: Generic drugs are chemically identical to brand-name versions but cost 80-85% less. With 12 monthly refills, a $35 copay difference becomes $420/year. When your doctor prescribes a brand-name drug, always ask if there's a generic.
shortcut: Annual saving per prescription = (brand copay − generic copay) × 12. For multiple prescriptions, sum the differences. Sometimes GoodRx cash price for generics is cheaper than insurance brand copay.
example:
Brand copay: $45
Generic copay: $10
Monthly diff: $35
Annual saving: $420

Two prescriptions switched to generic:
($35 + $20) × 12 = $660/year saved

title: Monthly payment vs total cost
concept: Dealers love to talk monthly payments because they sound affordable. But total cost = monthly payment × number of months. A $450/month payment over 72 months means you're paying $32,400 total. Always calculate the full cost before signing.
shortcut: Total cost = payment × months. Interest paid = total cost − loan amount. A $25,000 car at $450/month for 72 months costs $32,400 — that's $7,400 in interest.
example:
Loan: $25,000
Payment: $450/month × 72 months
Total: $32,400
Interest: $7,400

title: The hidden cost of '24 more months'
concept: Salespeople love long loan terms because they lower the monthly payment — and increase total interest. Extending from 48 to 72 months can drop your payment $130/month but add $3,800+ in total cost. Focus on the delta between terms, not the headline payment.
shortcut: Total cost difference = (payment_longer × months_longer) − (payment_shorter × months_shorter). Lower payment ≠ better deal. The extra months are pure interest extraction.
example:
Same $25,000 loan:
48 months × $550 = $26,400
72 months × $420 = $30,240
Extra cost of longer term: $3,840

Monthly 'savings' from 48→72: $130
Total cost increase: $3,840
The trade-off is bad.

title: Down payment math
concept: A down payment doesn't just reduce what you borrow — it eliminates interest on that money. Every $1 down saves you $1 + future interest. On a 5-year loan at 7%, a $5k down payment saves $5k principal + ~$900 interest = $5,900 in total cost.
shortcut: Down payment = price × down%. Loan = price − down. Interest saved by larger down ≈ extra down × loan rate × term/2. Quick rule: every $1 down saves $1.10-$1.20 on a 60-month loan.
example:
$30,000 car, 7% APR, 60 months:
0% down: $5,700 interest
20% down ($6,000): borrow $24k, $4,560 interest
Difference: $1,140 interest saved
Total savings: $7,140 over loan life

title: The 20/4/10 rule
concept: Financial experts recommend: 20% down payment, 4-year (48-month) max loan term, and total car costs under 10% of gross monthly income. This rule keeps you from being 'car poor' — spending so much on your car that it squeezes everything else.
shortcut: Max car cost (10% rule) = monthly gross income × 10%. That includes payment + insurance + gas. If you earn $5,000/month gross, max total car costs = $500/month.
example:
Monthly income: $5,000
10% max car cost: $500/month
Includes: payment + insurance + gas
If insurance + gas = $200
Max payment: $300/month

title: Car depreciation math
concept: New cars lose about 20% of their value in the first year and roughly 15% per year after that. A $35,000 car is worth about $28,000 after year one. Understanding depreciation helps you decide between new, certified pre-owned, and used.
shortcut: Value after year 1 = price × 80%. Value after year 2 ≈ year 1 value × 85%. Quick estimate: a car loses about half its value in 3-4 years.
example:
New car: $35,000
After year 1 (−20%): $28,000
After year 2 (−15%): $23,800
Lost $11,200 in 2 years

title: What your car really costs per month
concept: Monthly car cost ≠ monthly payment. The real number includes payment + insurance + gas + maintenance + depreciation. For most cars, that's $300-$400/month ON TOP of the payment. A $400 payment becomes a $700-$800/month total cost.
shortcut: Add payment + ~$150 insurance + ~$150 gas + ~$80 maintenance as baseline non-payment costs. Total monthly ownership = payment + $380 (typical). Add depreciation if you're tracking true cost.
example:
Payment: $400
Insurance: $150
Gas: $200
Maintenance: $80
Total monthly cost: $830

Reality: $830 × 12 = $9,960/year of car expenses, not $4,800.

title: Lease vs buy — the 3-year math
concept: Leasing: $350/month × 36 months = $12,600 spent, you own nothing at the end. Buying: $500/month × 60 months = $30,000, but after 36 months the car is worth ~$20,000. Your net 'cost' after 36 months: $30k payments − $20k value = $10k net. For the same 3 years, leasing cost you $2,600 more AND you have nothing to sell.
shortcut: Lease cost over term = monthly × months. Buy net cost over same term = (monthly × months) − resale value. Lower number wins. Buying almost always cheaper if you keep the car past the loan.
example:
Compare 3 years:
LEASE: $350 × 36 = $12,600 spent (own nothing)
BUY: $500 × 36 = $18,000 paid, car worth $20,000
Net: $18k − $20k = −$2,000 (you BUILT $2k equity)
Buying wins by $14,600 over 3 years

title: Is the dealer trade-in rip-off worth it?
concept: Dealers offer convenience but lowball trade-in prices. The spread between trade-in and private sale is typically $2,000-$4,000. Private selling takes time (2-4 weeks of effort) but the difference often comes out to $100-$200/hour of effort. Tax wrinkle: in most states, trading in reduces your sales tax base on the new car.
shortcut: Trade-in premium = private sale price − trade-in offer. Effective hourly = premium ÷ estimated hours of selling effort. Tax benefit of trade-in = (trade-in value) × your state sales tax rate.
example:
Car: $11,000 private market, $8,000 trade-in offer
Premium: $3,000
Estimated hours: 20 (photos, listings, calls, test drives, paperwork)
Effective: $150/hour

Tax benefit (trade-in): $8,000 × 8% = $640 less sales tax
Adjusted premium: $3,000 − $640 = $2,360

title: Student loan monthly payment
concept: Standard 10-year repayment costs about $100-$120 per $10,000 borrowed at typical 4-7% rates. A $30k loan ≈ $300-$360/month. A $50k loan ≈ $500-$600/month. This rule is accurate within 10% of the actual amortized payment.
shortcut: Per $10k borrowed at 4-7% APR over 10 years: ~$100-$120/month. Higher rate = closer to $120. Quick mental math: divide your balance by $10k, multiply by your per-$10k rate.
example:
Loan $40,000:
$40k ÷ $10k = 4
× $110 (~5% APR) = $440/month

Loan $25,000 at 6%:
2.5 × $115 = ~$287/month
Actual amortized: $278 (within $10)

title: Total cost of student loans
concept: Total repayment = monthly payment × number of months. Subtract the original loan to find total interest. A 10-year loan at 5-6% typically costs ~25-30% of original balance in interest. $40k loan? Expect $10k-$12k extra in interest.
shortcut: Total cost = payment × months. Interest = total − loan. Interest as % = interest ÷ loan × 100. Quick benchmark: 10-yr loan at 5-6% = ~28% interest premium.
example:
$30,000 loan, $318/mo × 120 months:
Total: $38,160
Interest: $8,160
Interest %: 27.2%

Within the 25-30% benchmark for standard repayment.

title: Refinancing savings
concept: Refinancing replaces your current loan with a new one at a lower interest rate. The savings come from the rate difference applied to your balance. Dropping from 6% to 4% on a $40,000 balance saves roughly $800/year in interest.
shortcut: Annual interest saving ≈ balance × (old rate − new rate). $40,000 × (6% − 4%) = $800/year. Over 10 years, that's $8,000 in savings — but you lose federal loan protections.
example:
Balance: $40,000
Old rate: 6%, New rate: 4%
Annual saving: $40,000 × 2% = $800
10-year saving: ~$8,000

title: Income-driven repayment
concept: Income-driven repayment (IDR) caps your monthly payment at a percentage of your discretionary income. The most common plan caps at 10% of income above 150% of the poverty line. Lower payments mean longer repayment and more total interest, but remaining balance is forgiven after 20-25 years.
shortcut: IDR payment ≈ (income − 150% of poverty line) × 10% / 12. If you earn $50,000 and poverty line for your size is $15,000: discretionary = $50,000 − $22,500 = $27,500. Monthly = $27,500 × 10% / 12 ≈ $229.
example:
Income: $50,000
150% poverty: $22,500
Discretionary: $27,500
10% of that / 12 months
IDR payment: ~$229/month

title: PSLF forgiveness math
concept: Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) forgives remaining federal loan balance after 120 qualifying payments (10 years) while working for a qualifying employer. The key math: total paid = IDR payment × 120 months. Forgiven amount = original balance + accrued interest − total paid.
shortcut: PSLF total paid = monthly IDR payment × 120. Forgiveness amount = remaining balance at month 120. If you pay $250/month for 10 years = $30,000 paid. If balance started at $80,000, you could get $50,000+ forgiven.
example:
Loan: $80,000
IDR payment: $250/month
10 years = $30,000 paid
Forgiven: $50,000+
(balance grew with interest)

title: Does your employer pay your student loans?
concept: Section 127 of the tax code lets employers contribute up to $5,250/year tax-free toward employee student loans. Made permanent under the OBBBA in 2025. As of 2025, 26% of employers offer this. That's equivalent to a $437.50/month tax-free raise that goes directly to your loan principal.
shortcut: Annual benefit ÷ 12 = monthly contribution to principal. Multi-year: benefit × years. Plus the interest you DON'T pay on principal that gets paid down earlier (rough: benefit × 4-6% × half the years).
example:
Employer max: $5,250/yr
Monthly: $437.50

5 years of full benefit:
$26,250 paid by employer
+ ~$2,000 in interest you don't pay
Total value: ~$28,250

title: Your loans are growing while you wait
concept: Unsubsidized federal loans accrue interest from disbursement. The 6-month grace period after graduation doesn't pause interest — it lets it pile up and capitalize (added to principal). A $25,000 loan at 5.5% accrues ~$680 in interest during grace alone. Most new grads don't realize this.
shortcut: Daily interest = balance × rate ÷ 365. Grace period total = daily × 180 days. Making interest-only payments during grace prevents capitalization and saves money long-term.
example:
$25,000 unsubsidized at 5.5%:
Daily interest: $3.77
Grace period (180 days): $678
New balance at repayment start: $25,678

Interest-only during grace ($113/mo):
Balance stays $25,000 → save $678 + future interest on it

title: Parent PLUS vs private — which costs less?
concept: Parent PLUS loans carry an 8.94% fixed rate + 4.228% origination fee (2025-26). Private parent loans start as low as 5.09% with no origination. For a parent with good credit, private can save $10k+ over 10 years on a $30k loan. But PLUS offers federal protections (IDR, deferment, PSLF) that private doesn't.
shortcut: Annual interest difference = balance × (PLUS rate − private rate). Over 10 years × 10. Origination fee adds to PLUS cost. Trade-off: ~$10k savings on private vs federal protections.
example:
$30,000 borrowed:
PLUS at 8.94%: ~$2,682/yr interest + $1,268 origination upfront
Private at 5.5%: ~$1,650/yr interest, no fee

Annual diff: ~$1,032
10-year diff: ~$10,320 + $1,268 = $11,588 saved with private
